title: Pub/sub
subtitle: One queue to split work, one queue per subscriber so everyone hears
mission: The cashier published 9 "OrderPaid" events. Kitchen, invoicing and loyalty need all of them. Analytics only showed up after the 6th. Wire the services to a shared queue or to one queue per service, and see who got what. Then try log mode, which keeps history.

predict.question: if kitchen, invoicing and loyalty read from the SAME queue, how many of the 9 events does each get?

feedback.right: right: in a queue, each message goes to one consumer only. The services become "competitors" and split the events like cooks sharing tickets. Great for splitting work, terrible for telling everyone.
feedback.wrong: each gets about 3: in a queue, each message is delivered to just one consumer. For every service to get everything, each needs its own queue bound to a fanout exchange (or, in Kafka, its own consumer group).
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run publish --queues shared and look at the table.

coach.ui: guess noted. Switch to the shared queue and compare the table.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run publish and then publish --queues shared.

tryNext.ui: Go back to "per service" and turn on log mode: analytics, which arrived late, reads from the start. (In Kafka a new group starts at the end by default, with auto.offset.reset=latest; reading from offset 0 needs auto.offset.reset=earliest.)
tryNext.cmd: Run publish --log yes and look at the analytics row (in Kafka, reading from offset 0 needs auto.offset.reset=earliest; the default is latest).

why.simples:
A shared queue is the kitchen’s ticket pile: each ticket goes to one cook only. It’s for splitting work.
Pub/sub is the family group chat: one message, and everyone gets their own copy. The publisher doesn’t know how many are listening.
And there’s the mailbox versus the bulletin board: in a queue, a read letter leaves the box; in a log (like Kafka), the note stays on the board and latecomers can still read it.
why.dev:
In RabbitMQ (AMQP 0-9-1), the producer publishes to an exchange, and bindings decide which queues get it. Types: direct (exact key), fanout (copies to every bound queue), topic (key pattern, like order.*) and headers. Pub/sub = a fanout or topic exchange with one queue per service; several consumers on the same queue = competing consumers.
In Kafka the same idea shows up as consumer groups: each group gets every message in the topic, and within a group the partitions are split among consumers. Same group splits; different groups copy.
why.especialista:
Queues and logs have different retention models. In a queue, an acked message is deleted; a new service only sees what arrives after its queue exists. In a log (Kafka, or RabbitMQ streams), messages stay for the retention time or size, and each reader keeps its offset: you can reprocess, and a new service can read history. Note: a new Kafka consumer group starts at the end of the topic by default (auto.offset.reset=latest); reading from offset 0 needs auto.offset.reset=earliest.
That changes architecture decisions: rebuilding a read model from events, auditing, debugging by replaying. In exchange, you manage retention, compaction, partitions and per-group lag. One queue per subscriber also multiplies storage: many subscribers on a big fanout is a sign to consider a stream.

mission.ui: time to break it: put everyone on the shared queue.
mission.cmd: time to break it: run publish --queues shared

break.success: Broken: on the same queue, each event went to just one service. The kitchen saw {kitchen} of 9, invoicing {invoice} and loyalty {loyalty}. Some paid pizzas were never made and some orders got no invoice.
break.calm: Each service with its own queue got all 9 events. Analytics got {analytics}. To break it, put everyone on the same queue.

ui: Choose how to wire the services and whether history is kept.
On the same queue, each message has a single destination.
cmd: The event name goes in quotes; --queues and --log are optional.

scene.label: Who got the 9 events
scene.caption: 9 events published; analytics subscribed after the 6th.
scene.sharedNote: A shared queue is for splitting work among copies of the SAME service, not for notifying different services.
scene.lateNote: With queues, latecomers only see what comes after: analytics got {analytics} of 9. History was already deleted.
scene.replayNote: In a log, messages stay for the retention period. Analytics started from offset 0 and read all 9. (In Kafka that needs auto.offset.reset=earliest: by default a new consumer group starts at the end, with latest.)

steps: With Docker installed, start RabbitMQ with the management UI: docker run -it --rm --name rabbitmq -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:4-management
Open http://localhost:15672 in your browser and log in with guest / guest (that user only works from your own machine, and is for study only).
Create an exchange eventos of type fanout and two queues, cozinha and nota. On each queue, bind it to the eventos exchange.
On the eventos exchange page, publish 3 messages. Then look at both queues’ counts.

To see the other side, publish 6 messages to the pedidos queue (the one from lesson 1). In worker.py from the ack lesson, change to basic_qos(prefetch_count=1) (otherwise the first worker grabs all 6 at once) and run two copies, in two terminals, reading the same pedidos queue: they split the messages.
recipe.ok: the cozinha and nota queues show 3 messages each, from a single publish per message; and the two worker copies on the same queue print different messages.
